title: Newly Discovered Canadian Citizenship: How to Sponsor Your Spouse for Permanent Residence
excerpt: Citizenship by descent follows bloodlines, not marriage — but as a Canadian citizen you can sponsor your spouse or partner for PR, leading eventually to citizenship.
body:
• Discovering you are a Canadian citizen by descent gives you the full rights of citizenship — including the right to sponsor a spouse or partner for permanent residence — but it does not automatically extend to your spouse.
  • Sponsorship leads to Canadian permanent residence, not immediate citizenship; a permanent resident can apply for citizenship after accumulating three years of physical presence in Canada within a five-year period.
  • Sponsors must be at least 18, must not be on social assistance (other than for disability), and must show they can support the family and plan to live in Canada.
  • Couples can apply through the inland or outland stream, and Quebec runs its own separate second-step process on top of the federal one.

Finding out you are a Canadian citizen by descent — perhaps through a parent or grandparent born in Canada — is life-changing news. It opens the right to live, work and travel freely in Canada, and to pass citizenship on to your own children. But if you are married, one question arrives almost immediately: does any of this extend to your spouse?

The short answer is yes, but not automatically. Canadian citizenship by descent follows bloodlines, not marriage, so your spouse's status stays exactly what it was before you received your certificate. The good news is that your new legal status gives you the same sponsorship rights as any other Canadian citizen: you can sponsor your spouse or partner for Canadian permanent residence through a well-established process.

Residence First, Citizenship Later

It is important to understand what sponsorship actually delivers. Sponsoring a spouse or partner leads to Canadian permanent residence, not citizenship. Permanent residence carries most of the day-to-day rights of citizenship — the ability to live, work and study anywhere in the country. After meeting the residency requirement, generally three years of physical presence in Canada within a five-year period, the permanent resident can then apply for Canadian citizenship.

The same path is available whether your partner is legally married to you, your common-law partner (someone you have lived with in a marriage-like relationship for at least 12 months) or your conjugal partner (a couple together for at least a year who could not live together or marry because of circumstances beyond their control, such as immigration barriers or legal restrictions).

What You Need to Qualify as a Sponsor

To sponsor a spouse or partner, you must be at least 18 years old. If you are not already living in Canada, you need to show that you plan to move there by the time your spouse becomes a permanent resident. You must also demonstrate that you are not receiving social assistance for reasons other than disability, and that you can cover the basic needs of yourself, your partner and any dependent children included in the application.

Certain circumstances can limit your ability to sponsor. A history of specific criminal convictions, particularly violent offences, is one of them. If anything in your background is unclear, a licensed immigration lawyer who specialises in citizenship and sponsorship cases is worth consulting before you apply.

Inland or Outland: Two Routes

The process differs slightly depending on where you both live. If your spouse lives outside Canada, you typically apply under the Family Class, commonly called outland sponsorship. Canadian citizens sponsoring a spouse or conjugal partner can pursue outland sponsorship even from within Canada, which preserves their freedom to travel during processing — something the inland stream does not allow. Conjugal partners must use the outland class.

If you both live in Canada, the application usually goes through the Spouse or Common-Law Partner in Canada Class — inland sponsorship. One practical advantage of inland: your partner may be eligible for an open work permit while the permanent residence application is being processed, allowing them to work legally well before a final decision.

Wherever you marry, the marriage must be legally recognised both in Canada and in the country where the ceremony took place. For Americans who married in the US and are only now discovering Canadian citizenship, the marriage certificate from that state or jurisdiction is what immigration officials will look for.

A New Rule on Passing Citizenship to Children

One recent change is worth noting for new citizens thinking about family planning. Children born or adopted on or after December 15, 2025, face an additional requirement: their Canadian citizen parent must show at least 1,095 days of physical presence in Canada before the child's birth or adoption for the child to receive citizenship by descent. Biological children can otherwise claim citizenship through the same line of descent as their parent; adopted children may qualify too, though the process can involve an extra step.

Paperwork, Medicals and Quebec

Once you know which class applies, the application package, checklists and forms are available online, and the documentation required is substantial — covering both the sponsor's side and the partner's application for permanent residence. Every family member included who is not already a Canadian citizen or permanent resident will need a medical exam at a designated point in processing.

If you plan to settle in Quebec, expect a second step: after federal officials confirm your eligibility as a sponsor, you must complete a separate application with Quebec's immigration ministry, which has its own conditions on residency, financial capacity and criminal history. The overall timeline runs longer for Quebec-bound couples.

Criminal inadmissibility — for example, a DUI conviction — can complicate a spouse's application, but it is not always disqualifying. Depending on the offence and how much time has passed, it may be possible to overcome it through routes such as criminal rehabilitation.

Why This Matters to the Diaspora

For many Indian-origin families in the United States, Canadian citizenship by descent is a genuine discovery: a parent or grandparent born in Canada, a childhood detail never formalised. In an era of tightening US visa rules and rising H-1B fees, that newly confirmed citizenship — and the ability to bring a spouse along through sponsorship — can reshape a family's entire immigration strategy. The road is longer than simply claiming your own citizenship, but for couples who want to build a life in Canada together, sponsorship remains a reliable path forward.
